Equation

8
. We show that there exists a decomposition of
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
into
2
connected components. Consider the following sets of vertices

\displaystyle C

\displaystyle\coloneqq\{i\in[n]\mid P{|{i}\rangle}={|{i}\rangle}\},

\displaystyle C^{\bot}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\{i\in[n]\mid P{|{i}\rangle}=0\},

\displaystyle C^{\sim}

\displaystyle\coloneqq[n]\setminus(C\cup C^{\bot}).

Clearly,
C,C^{\bot},C^{\sim}
partition
[n]
. We show that edges of
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
can only exist inside these sets. Let
i\sim j
. We have to exclude the following cases.

•

i\in C
,
j\in C^{\bot}
: In this case we have
P{|{i}\rangle}={|{i}\rangle}\neq 0
and
P^{\bot}{|{j}\rangle}={|{j}\rangle}
, so the
A
-term is non-zero. This already excludes classical edges. We moreover have
P{|{j}\rangle}=0
, so the
C
-term is zero and thus cannot cancel out the
A
contribution. This excludes strange edges as well.

•

i\in C
,
j\in C^{\sim}
: In this case we have
P{|{i}\rangle}={|{i}\rangle}\neq 0
and
P^{\bot}{|{j}\rangle}\neq 0
, which excludes classical edges. We also have
P^{\bot}{|{i}\rangle}=0
, so the
C
-term is zero. This excludes strange edges.

•

i\in C^{\bot}
,
j\in C^{\sim}
: Follows from the previous case by considering the condition with
P\leftrightarrow P^{\bot}
exchanged.

The cases with
i
and
j
exchanged are follow by undirectedness.
Finally, we show that there cannot be any classical edges inside
C^{\sim}
. Indeed,
i,j\in C^{\sim}
implies
P{|{i}\rangle}\not\in\{0,{|{i}\rangle}\}
and
P{|{j}\rangle}\not\in\{0,{|{j}\rangle}\}
, and thus also
P^{\bot}{|{j}\rangle}\not\in\{0,{|{j}\rangle}\}
. It follows that the
A
-term is non-zero and thus the condition unsatisfiable for classical edges.

Now by assumption,
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
has at least one classical edge. This implies that either
C
or
C^{\bot}
must be non-empty. Without loss of generality assume
C
is non-empty. Then
C
and
C^{\bot}\cup C^{\sim}
partition
[n]
and by our previous observations there is no edge between the two sets. It follows that
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
is disconnected, which completes the proof.
∎

by vectors
\psi_{k+1},\dots,\psi_{n}
. We define a unitary matrix
H
by
H_{is}=\braket{\psi_{s}|i}
. The fact that
P
has full coordinate support implies that every row of
H
has at least one non-zero entry in the first
k
columns.

Equation

11
now implies

\sum_{s=1}^{k}\braket{\psi_{s}|i}{|{\psi_{s}}\rangle}=P{|{i}\rangle}=\alpha P{|{j}\rangle}=\alpha\sum_{s=1}^{k}\braket{\psi_{s}|j}{|{\psi_{s}}\rangle}.

Since the
\psi_{s}
are orthogonal, this is only the case if

H_{is}=\braket{\psi_{s}|i}=\alpha\braket{\psi_{s}|j}=\alpha H_{js}.

for all
s\leq k
. Similarly, by
Equation

12
we have

\sum_{t=k+1}^{n}\braket{\overline{\psi_{t}}|j}{|{\overline{\psi_{t}}}\rangle}=\overline{P^{\bot}}{|{j}\rangle}=\beta\overline{P^{\bot}}{|{i}\rangle}=\beta\sum_{t=k+1}^{n}\braket{\overline{\psi_{t}}|i}{|{\overline{\psi_{t}}}\rangle},

which implies

\overline{H}_{jt}=\braket{\overline{\psi_{t}}|j}=\beta\braket{\overline{\psi_{t}}|i}=\beta\overline{H}_{it}.

for all
k<t\leq n
. We thus conclude that

\frac{H_{is}}{H_{js}}=\frac{\overline{H}_{it}}{\overline{H}_{jt}}c_{ij}\qquad\textsc{and}\qquad\frac{H_{jt}}{H_{it}}=\frac{\overline{H}_{js}}{\overline{H}_{is}}\overline{c_{ij}}

for all
s\leq k
,
k<t\leq n
whenever
i\sim j
. This means that if
i\sim j
, the rows
H_{i*}
and
H_{j*}
split into two parts: the first
k
columns and the last
n-k
columns, which are respectively scalar multiples of each other. Call this property (M). Since
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
is connected and
n\geq 3
, there are at least three vertices connected by a path. It follows that the corresponding rows must satisfy property (M). We show that no unitary matrix satisfies this constraint.

Claim 1
.

Let
x,x^{\prime}
be a pair of rows of a unitary matrix that satisfy property (M). Suppose
x
splits into
x_{1}
and
x_{2}
. Then
x_{2}\neq 0
.

Proof.

Suppose otherwise. Since
H
is unitary,
x
and
x^{\prime}
are orthogonal. We thus have

x^{\prime}_{1}x_{1}^{\dagger}=x^{\prime}_{1}x_{1}^{\dagger}+x^{\prime}_{2}x_{2}^{\dagger}=x^{\prime}x^{\dagger}=0
, but
x_{1}
is a scalar multiple of
x^{\prime}_{1}
by property (M), so their inner product cannot be
0
.
∎

Claim 2
.

Let
k<n
and
H
be a unitary matrix such that every row has at least one non-zero entry in the first
k
columns. Then
H
does not contain three rows that pairwise satisfy property (M).

Proof.

Assume for contradiction that there are rows
u,v,w
pairwise satisfying property (M). This means that

\displaystyle v_{1}=\alpha u_{1}

\displaystyle\quad\textsc{and}\quad v_{2}=\beta u_{2}

\displaystyle w_{1}=\gamma u_{1}

\displaystyle\quad\textsc{and}\quad w_{2}=\delta u_{2}

Since
H
is unitary, they must be mutually orthogonal. It follows that

\displaystyle\overline{\alpha}\lVert u_{1}\rVert^{2}+\overline{\beta}\lVert u_{2}\rVert^{2}=u_{1}(\alpha u_{1})^{\dagger}+u_{2}(\beta u_{2})^{\dagger}=uv^{\dagger}=0

\displaystyle\overline{\gamma}\lVert u_{1}\rVert^{2}+\overline{\delta}\lVert u_{2}\rVert^{2}=u_{1}(\gamma u_{1})^{\dagger}+u_{2}(\delta u_{2})^{\dagger}=uw^{\dagger}=0

Set
\xi=\lVert u_{1}\rVert^{2}/\lVert u_{2}\rVert^{2}
. Note that this is well-defined since
u_{2}\neq 0
by
1
. It is moreover positive, since by assumption
u_{1}
contains at least one non-zero entry. Substituting
\xi
into the orthogonality equations yields

\beta=-\xi\alpha\quad\textsc{and}\quad\delta=-\xi\gamma.

(13)

Now consider the remaining orthogonality constraint, which yields

\alpha\overline{\gamma}\lVert u_{1}\rVert^{2}+\beta\overline{\delta}\lVert u_{2}\rVert^{2}=\alpha u_{1}\cdot(\gamma u_{1})^{\dagger}+\beta u_{2}\cdot(\delta u_{2})^{\dagger}=vw^{\dagger}=0.

By
Equation

13
this is equivalent to

\alpha\overline{\gamma}\lVert u_{1}\rVert^{2}+(-\xi\alpha)(-\xi\overline{\gamma})\lVert u_{2}\rVert^{2}=\alpha\overline{\gamma}\lVert u_{1}\rVert^{2}+\xi^{2}\alpha\overline{\gamma}\lVert u_{2}\rVert^{2}=0

Dividing both sides by
\alpha\overline{\gamma}\lVert u_{2}\rVert^{2}
leaves us with

\xi+\xi^{2}=0,

but this is unsatisfiable for positive
\xi
, contradiction.
∎

We have seen that
Equation

10
is only satisfied for all
i,j\in[n]
if the unitary matrix
H=(\braket{\psi_{s}|i})_{is}
contains at least three rows that pairwise satisfy property (M). But
H
satisfies the constraints of
2
and thus cannot contain such a collection of rows. This is a contradiction, so
X_{A,B,C}
must be connected.
∎

4.2
Colouring

We now move on to colouring. Recall that a quantum graph is
k
-colourable if there exist
k
non-zero projectors
P_{1},\dots,P_{k}
on
\mathbb{C}^{n}
that sum to the identity, such that

G
P_{s}
=
0
P_{s}

for all
s\in[k]
. There is a trivial lower bound: Every quantum graph can be at most
1
colourable, which is satisfied if and only if
G
is the zero map. However, contrary to the case of connected components, there is no trivial upper bound on the number of colours that are needed. We will see that there are quantum graphs that are not colourable at all.

4.2.1
ABC Graphs

Since the colouring condition is very similar to that for connected components, it is unsurprising that we can also prove a splitting principle for colouring. In fact, it is proved the exact same way we did for connected components in
Section

4.1.2
, so we refrain from repeating the proof here. Merely the conclusion for the chromatic number is different. The splitting principle for colouring states that a collection of projectors is a colouring for
X_{A,B,C}
if and only if it is a colouring for both
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}
and
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
. While for the number of connected components we were interested in the maximum possible number of projectors, the chromatic number is equal to the minimum number of projectors needed. We thus obtain the following result.

Proposition 4.16
.

We have
\chi(X_{A,B,C})\geq\max\{\chi(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}),\chi(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B})\}
.

Similarly, an analogous argument as for connected components shows that every
k
-colouring of the strange graph
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
induces a
k
-colouring of
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}
.

Proposition 4.17
.

For all
k\in\mathbb{N}
it holds that if
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
is
k
-colourable then so is
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}
. In particular, we have
\chi(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C})\leq\chi(\mathfrak{G}(A,C))
.

Proof.

Let
C_{1},\dots,C_{k}
be the colour classes of a
k
-colouring of
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
. We set

P_{s}=\sum_{i\in C_{i}}{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{i}.

Then the
P_{s}
are orthogonal projectors summing to the identity and the condition

\mathring{A}
+
\mathring{C}
P_{s}
P_{s}
P_{s}
P_{s}
=
0

becomes

Since
C_{s}
is a colour class, we have
ii^{\prime}\not\in E(\mathfrak{G}(A,C))
for all
i\neq i^{\prime}\in C_{s}
and thus
A_{ii^{\prime}}=C_{i^{\prime}i}=0
as desired. For
i=i^{\prime}
, we have
\mathring{A}_{ii^{\prime}}=\mathring{C}_{ii^{\prime}}=0
by definition. This completes the proof.
∎

Note that unlike the corresponding result for connected components, this result only holds for ABC graphs with trivial
B
. This is related to the splitting principle: In the case of connected components we were lucky that our translation of the connected components of
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
also happened to be a decomposition into connected components of
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
. We have no such luck for colouring. While it would generally be possible that there exists a different translation that does work, the next section will show that this is not the case.

4.2.2
AB Graphs

The first observation we make is that AB graphs can be arbitrarily difficult to colour.

Proposition 4.18
.

There exist quantum graphs of the form
X_{A,B}
that are not colourable.

Proof.

Recall that the complete graph
K_{n}
satisfies

K_{n}=X_{\tfrac{nJ-I}{n},\tfrac{nI-J}{n}}

and is thus of the form
X_{A,B}
. However, it is not colourable: The colouring condition reads

but the left-hand side has rank
1
, while the right-hand side has rank
n\cdot\rk P_{s}
. This is unsatisfiable for
n\geq 2
.
∎

Since every strange graph is at least
n
-colourable, this shows that
Proposition

4.17
cannot be generalised to non-trivial
B
. This is a symptom of the colourings for
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}
and
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
generally being incompatible; it is not exclusively caused by
B
. Indeed,
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
is always at least
n
-colourable.

Proposition 4.19
.

Every quantum graph of the form
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
is
n
-colourable.

(14)

Now let
v_{1},\dots,v_{n}
be the orthonormal DFT basis of
\mathbb{C}^{n}
, that is the
k
th entry of
v_{j}
is
\exp(jk\cdot 2\mathrm{i}\pi/n)/\sqrt{n}
. Let
P_{s}={|{v_{s}}\rangle}\!\bra{v_{s}}
. Plugging in
\overline{v_{i}}
into the bottom left- and
v_{j}
into the bottom right of
Equation

14
yields
0
if
i\neq s
or
j\neq s
, and
B\circ m(\overline{v_{s}}\otimes v_{s})
otherwise. Since
m
is entrywise multiplication on
\mathbb{C}^{n}
and the entries of
v_{s}
have norm
1
, we have
m(\overline{v_{s}}\otimes v_{s})=\mathbf{1}
. Since we assume
B
to be loopless, we have
B\mathbf{1}=0
, and thus
B\circ m(\overline{v_{s}}\otimes v_{s})=0
. Since both the
\overline{v_{i}}
and the
v_{i}
form a basis, we conclude that
Equation

14
holds.
∎

In this case, the colourability is limited by the dimension of the kernel of
B
.

Proposition 4.20
.

It holds that
\chi(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B})\geq n/\dim\ker B
.

Let
T_{s}=\img P_{s}
. The condition requires that the subspaces
T_{s}^{2}=\lspan\{m(\overline{v}\otimes w)\mid v,w\in T_{s}\}
must be contained in the kernel of
B
. Now suppose there existed a
k
-colouring
P_{1},\dots,P_{k}
of
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
. Since the
P_{s}
sum to the identity, there needs to exist an
s
such that
\rk P_{s}\geq n/k
. We claim that
\dim T_{s}^{2}\geq\dim T_{s}
, and thus
\dim\ker B\geq n/k
.

Without loss of generality assume that for all
j\in[n]
there exists a
v\in T_{s}
such that
v_{j}\neq 0
. Otherwise we consider
T_{s}
as a subspace of
\mathbb{C}^{m}
for some suitable
m<n
.

Claim 1
.

There exists a
w\in T_{s}
such that
w_{j}\neq 0
for all
j\in[n]
.

Proof.

Choose some arbitrary
w^{(0)}\in T_{s}
. Let
i
be minimal with
w^{(0)}_{i}=0
. By assumption, there exists a
u\in T_{s}
such that
u_{i}\neq 0
. Let

\alpha\coloneqq\max_{i}\lvert w^{(0)}_{i}\rvert\qquad\quad\beta\coloneqq\min\{\lvert u_{i}\rvert\mid u_{i}\neq 0\}\qquad\quad\gamma\coloneqq\inf\{r\in R^{+}\mid r\beta>\alpha\},

and set
w^{(1)}=w^{(0)}+ru
. Then
w^{(1)}\in T_{s}
,
w^{(1)}_{i}\neq 0
and for all
j\in[n]
,
w^{(0)}_{j}\neq 0
implies
w^{(1)}_{j}\neq 0
. Iterating this procedure for at most
n
steps yields the desired
w
.
∎

Let
w
be as in the claim and observe that
T_{s}^{2}\supseteq\{m(\overline{v}\otimes w)\mid v\in T_{s}\}
. Recall that
m
is componentwise multiplication, and thus
m(\overline{v}\otimes w)=\overline{v}\bullet w
. This in turn is equal to
W\overline{v}
for
W=\diag w
. Now
\dim T_{s}=\dim\overline{T_{s}}
and
W
is invertible. It follows that

\dim T_{s}^{2}\geq\dim\{m(\overline{v}\otimes w)\mid v\in T_{s}\}=\dim\{Wv\mid v\in\overline{T_{s}}\}=\dim\overline{T_{s}}=\dim T_{s}

as desired. As shown above, this implies that
\dim\ker B\geq\dim T_{s}^{2}\geq\dim T_{s}\geq n/k
for any
k
-colouring. In particular, for an optimal
\chi(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B})
-colouring, we get

\chi(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B})\geq\frac{n}{\dim\ker B}

as desired.
∎

For
A
alone, we recover precisely the chromatic number.

Proposition 4.21
.

For all
k\in\mathbb{N}
, it holds that
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
is
k
-colourable if and only if
A
is.

Proof.

Proposition

4.17
and
Proposition

3.19
establish that
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
is
k
-colourable if
A
is. Conversely, suppose that
P_{1},\dots,P_{k}
are a
k
-colouring of
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
. Then per definition, we have

\mathring{A}
P_{s}
P_{s}
=
0

for all
s\in[k]
. This is equivalent to

\mathring{A}
P_{s}
P_{s}
i
j
=
0

for all
i,j\in[n]
. We can simplify the (co)multiplications, which yields

\lxSVG@closescope }{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-66.36395pt}{-23.66498pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-3.8889pt}{-1.83437pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}

{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{18.83957pt}{-3.22221pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\hss}\lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}.

This in turn is only satisfied if
A_{ij}\neq 0
implies
P{|{i}\rangle}=0
or
P{|{j}\rangle}=0
. Let
C_{1},\dots,C_{k}\subseteq[n]
be defined as

C_{s}=\{i\in[n]\mid P_{s}{|{i}\rangle}=0\}^{c}

The
C_{s}
are valid colour classes: Assume for contradiction that there were
i,j\in C_{s}
with
i\sim j
. Then
A_{ij}\neq 0
and thus
P_{s}{|{i}\rangle}=0
or
P_{s}{|{j}\rangle}=0
. This implies that
i\not\in C_{s}
or
j\not\in C_{s}
, contradicting our assumption. They also cover
[n]
. Suppose there was some
x\in[n]
such that
x\not\in C_{s}
for all
s
. Then we have
P_{s}{|{x}\rangle}=0
for all
s
and thus

{|{x}\rangle}=I{|{x}\rangle}=\sum_{s}P_{s}{|{x}\rangle}=0\neq{|{x}\rangle}.

We have proved that there exist colour classes
C_{1},\dots,C_{k}
that jointly cover
[n]
. To obtain a graph colouring, we let

\tilde{C}_{s}=C_{s}\setminus\bigcup_{t>s}C_{t}

Then the
\tilde{C}_{s}
form a partition of
[n]
and we have
\tilde{C}_{s}\subseteq C_{s}
, so the colouring condition is still satisfied. Consequently,
\tilde{C}_{1},\dots,\tilde{C}_{k}
is a
k
-colouring of
A
.
∎

4.2.3
The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Cases

We now turn our attention to the Symmetric and Antisymmetric quantum graphs. The Antisymmetric quantum graph turns out to be
n
-colourable, which we show by another rank-based argument.

Proposition 4.22
.

It holds that
\chi(G^{\mathrm{asym}})=n
.

Proof.

In
Proposition

3.13
we have seen that
G^{\mathrm{asym}}
is of the form
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}
, and by
Proposition

3.18
its corresponding strange graph is the complete graph of strange edges with phase
\pi
.
Proposition

4.17
thus implies that
\chi(G^{\mathrm{asym}})\leq n
. On the other hand, the colouring condition for
G^{\mathrm{asym}}

The left-hand side has rank

, while the right-hand side has rank

. The only way to satisfy the equation is thus when
\rk P_{s}=1
for all

, which implies that
\chi(G^{\mathrm{asym}})\geq n
.
∎

For the Symmetric quantum graph we find a similar situation as for the connected components of
G^{\mathrm{asym}}
, where
n=2
is a special case. We also find that for
n\geq 3
,
G^{\mathrm{sym}}
is not colourable at all.

Proposition 4.23
.

For
n=2

is

Note that the right-hand side has rank
n\cdot\rk P_{s}
, while the left-hand side has rank at most
1+(\rk P_{s})^{2}
. An elementary computation shows that this is only compatible if
n=2
or
\rk P_{s}=n
. Suppose
n\neq 2
and
\rk P_{s}=n
. The only projector of rank
n
is the identity, in which case the right-hand side becomes a multiple of the identity on
\mathbb{C}^{n}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{n}
, while the left-hand side becomes the projector onto the symmetric subspace of
\mathbb{C}^{n}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{n}
. These are obviously different maps, so the equality cannot be satisfied for
n\neq 2
. It follows that
G^{\mathrm{sym}}
is not colourable for
n\geq 3
.

On the other hand, suppose
n=2
. We know that
P_{s}\not\in\{0,I\}
, so we must have
\rk P_{s}=1
. This means that we can rewrite the condition equivalently as

We can factor the
P_{s}
term, in which case the condition simplifies to

\frac{1}{2}({|{\overline{\psi_{s}}}\rangle}\!\bra{\overline{\psi_{s}}}+{|{\psi_{s}}\rangle}\!\bra{\psi_{s}})=\frac{1}{2}I,

which is satisfied for
\psi_{s}=({|{1}\rangle}+i{|{2}\rangle})/\sqrt{2}
.
∎

4.2.4
The Complete and Empty Graphs

The cases of the complete and empty graphs are now straightforward. Since the adjacency operator of
K_{n}^{c}
is the zero map, the identity satisfies the colouring condition, which implies that
\chi(K_{n}^{c})=1
. On the other hand, we have shown in
Proposition

4.18
that the complete graph
K_{n}
is not colourable at all. This concludes our investigation of the chromatic number.

Proposition 4.24
.

We have
\chi(K_{n}^{c})=1
, while
K_{n}
is not colourable.

4.2.5
Notes on (Non-)Colourability of Quantum Graphs

We have seen that there exist quantum graphs that are not classically colourable. On first glance, this might seem like a flaw in the definition of
k
-colourability. We argue that this is not the case: the obstruction is intrinsic to the non-commutativity of the quantum edge space. A classical
k
-colouring requires orthogonal projections
P_{1},\dots,P_{k}
summing to the identity and satisfying
P_{s}XP_{s}=0
for every
X\in S
. For quantum graphs whose adjacency operator has large rank (see
Proposition

4.18
, where the colouring condition leads to an irreconcilable rank mismatch) no non-zero projection can satisfy this simultaneously for all edges. This is natural: In the classical setting, adjacency matrices have entries in
\{0,1\}
and one can always assign one colour per vertex. For quantum graphs, however, the edge space
S
can be non-commutatively too dense for any classical partition of the identity to separate.

In
[
8
]
, see also
[
18
]
, the authors also propose a definition of quantum colouring. While the colouring notion we used so far corresponds to the existence of a
classical
winning strategy in a suitably chosen non-local game played on the quantum graph, quantum colourings correspond to
quantum
strategies. More precisely, the classical chromatic number
\chi
restricts to an ancilla algebra
\mathcal{N}=\mathbb{C}
, whereas the quantum chromatic number
\chi_{q}
allows any finite-dimensional von Neumann algebra
\mathcal{N}
. The entanglement encoded in
\mathcal{N}
provides the players with shared quantum resources, enabling correlations that are impossible classically and making every quantum graph on
M_{n}
finitely colourable.

Proposition 4.25

(Theorem 6.6. in
[
8
]
)
.

For every quantum graph
G
on
M_{n}
, we have
\chi_{q}(G)\leq n^{2}
.

The bound
n^{2}
is tight: It holds that
\chi_{q}(K_{n})=n^{2}=\dim M_{n}

[
8
,
18
]
. By constrast, we have seen in
Proposition

4.18
that
K_{n}
is not classically colourable. In particular,
K_{n}
exhibits a strict separation

\chi(K_{n})=\infty\;>\;n^{2}=\chi_{q}(K_{n}),

demonstrating that quantum entanglement yields a decisive advantage in the colouring game for quantum graphs. The
n^{2}
projections achieving the quantum colouring are given by a “shift and multiply” unitary error basis for
M_{n}
, see
[
8
, Theorem 6.6]
for details.

4.3
Independent Sets

Recall that the notion of independent sets for quantum graphs was introduced in
Definition

2.16
via the operator space point of view: A
k
-independent set
of a quantum graph
G
is a projector
P\in M_{n}
of rank
k
such that
PSP\subseteq\mathbb{C}P
, where
S
is the operator space associated to
G
. Clearly, any rank one projector
P={|{v}\rangle}\!\bra{v}
has this property, hence every quantum graph
G
has
\alpha(G)\geq 1
.

Before moving on to the study of the independent sets of quantum graphs with symmetry, let us comment on the fact that the independent set condition from
Definition

2.16
is very close to the notion of
isotropic subspace
introduced in
[
3
]
: A subspace
U\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{n}
is an isotropic subspace of an alternating matrix space

\mathcal{A}\subseteq\{X\in M_{n}\,:\,X^{\top}=-X\}

if, for any
A\in\mathcal{A}
and any
u,u^{\prime}\in U
, we have
u^{\mathsf{T}}Au^{\prime}=0
. Comparing this definition with the independent set definition in our work, we spot two important differences:

•

On the one hand, we only require that
PSP
is a multiple of
P
, not necessarily
PSP=0
as in the definition of the isotropic subspace from
[
3
]
.

•

On the other hand, we work exclusively in the complex case scenario, so the forms we are considering are sesquilinear, not bilinear: We would work with conditions of the form
u^{\dagger}Au^{\prime}=0
instead of
u^{\mathsf{T}}Au^{\prime}=0
.

Although not strictly equivalent, these conditions are closely related: In
[
3
, Theorem 1.3]
, the authors show that the independence number of a graph
G
is equal to the maximum dimension of an isotropic subspace of the alternating matrix space
\mathcal{A}(G)=\{{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}-{|{j}\rangle}\!\bra{i}\mid i\sim j\}
, a result similar to our
Proposition

4.28
. Note that
\mathcal{A}(G)
is precisely the operator space associated to
X_{G/2,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},-G/2}
. A similar comment applies to the case of the coloring graph parameters.

X_{A,B,C}
splits into independent conditions for the
AC
part and the
B
part. Indeed, a projector
P

For
i\neq j
, the
B
-term is zero and we recover the independent set condition for
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}
. For
i=j
, we have
\mathring{A}_{ji}=\mathring{C}_{ij}=0
, and we recover the independent set condition for
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
. It thus follows that an independent set for
X_{A,B,C}
must simultaneously be an independent set of
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}
and
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
. We thus get the following result.

Proposition 4.26
.

We have
\alpha(X_{A,B,C})\leq\min\{\alpha(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}C}),\alpha(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}))\}
.

For the independence number, this result is particularly useful, since we can determine
\alpha(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C})
exactly.

Proposition 4.27
.

For quantum graphs of the form
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}
we have
\alpha(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C})=\alpha(\mathfrak{G}(A,C))
.

Proof.

We first show that
\alpha(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C})\geq\alpha(\mathfrak{G}(A,C))
. We show the stronger results that every independent set of
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
induces an independent set of
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}C}
of the same size. By realigning, we find that the projector onto the operator space corresponding to
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}
is given by

be an independent set of

(16)

We now choose our independent set as
X=\{i\in[n]\mid P{|{i}\rangle}=0\}^{c}
. Then we have
\lvert X\rvert\geq n-\dim\ker P=\rk P=k
. Suppose then that
i\sim j
in
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
. If
Equation

16
is satsfied for
c_{ij}=0
then it is straightforward to see that either
P{|{i}\rangle}=0
or
P{|{j}\rangle}=0
and thus
i\not\in X
or
j\not\in X
. Suppose then that the equation is satisfied for
c_{ij}\neq 0
. Dividing by
c_{ij}
yields

\alpha P{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}P+\beta P{|{j}\rangle}\!\bra{i}P=P.

Since
P
is a projector, we must have

\displaystyle(\alpha P{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}P+\beta P{|{j}\rangle}\!\bra{i}P)^{2}

\displaystyle=\alpha^{2}P_{ji}P{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}P+\alpha\beta P_{jj}P{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{i}P+\beta\alpha P_{ii}P{|{j}\rangle}\!\bra{j}P+\beta^{2}P_{ij}P{|{j}\rangle}\!\bra{i}P

\displaystyle=\alpha P{|{i}\rangle}\big(\alpha P_{ji}\bra{j}P+\beta P_{jj}\bra{i}P\big)+\beta P{|{j}\rangle}\big(\beta P_{ij}\bra{i}P+\alpha P_{ii}\bra{j}P\big)

\displaystyle\overset{!}{=}\alpha P{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}P+\beta P{|{j}\rangle}\!\bra{i}P

Since
i\sim j
, we know that
\alpha=\mathring{A}_{ji}/c_{ij}\neq 0
. The equation is thus only satisfied if
\beta=0
,
P_{jj}=0
, or
\bra{i}P=0
. If
\bra{i}P=0
we have
P{|{i}\rangle}=0
and thus
i\not\in X
. If
P_{jj}=0
, then
\lVert P{|{j}\rangle}\rVert^{2}=\bra{j}PP{|{j}\rangle}=\bra{j}P{|{j}\rangle}=0
and thus
P{|{j}\rangle}=0
and
j\not\in X
. Suppose then that
\beta=0
. Then we have

P=\alpha P{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}P,

which implies that
\rk P=1
, contradicting our assumption. It follows that
X
is indeed an independent set, which completes the proof.
∎

4.3.2
AB Graphs

An immediate corollary of
Proposition

4.27
is that the independence number of
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
coincides with that of
A
.

Proposition 4.28
.

It holds that
\alpha(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})=\alpha(A)
.

Proof.

By
Proposition

3.19
we have
A\cong\mathfrak{G}(A,\makebox[4.30554pt]{{$\cdot$}})
and by
Proposition

4.27
we have
\alpha(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})=\alpha(\mathfrak{G}(A,\makebox[4.30554pt]{{$\cdot$}}))
.
∎

While we cannot determine the independence number of
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
precisely, we can give strong bounds. We will see that the bounds are not only tight, but the upper and lower bounds coincide for certain
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
. Concretely, it turns out that the independence number is closely related to both the rank of
B
and the matrix representation of
B
in the standard basis.

Definition 4.29
.

Let
X
be an
n\times n
matrix. We denote by

\operatorname{EqRows}(X)\coloneqq\max\{k\in[n]\mid\exists j_{1}<\cdots<j_{k}\in[n],X_{j_{1}*}=X_{j_{2}*}=\dots=X_{j_{k}*}\}

the maximum number of equal rows of
X
.

}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{20.4034pt}{-2.5pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-28.45276pt}{0.0pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

\hss}\lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}\kern 5.0pt.

(17)

Let
D_{i}\colon\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
be left-multiplication by
B{|{i}\rangle}
. Then in the standard basis, we have
D_{i}=\diag(B{|{i}\rangle})
, and equation
Equation

17
becomes

PD_{i}P=\beta_{i}P.

(18)

This phrasing of the independence condition suggests to construct
P
explicitly as follows.

Proposition 4.30
.

Let
B
be a projector. Every set of equal rows of
B
induces an independent set of
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
.

Proof.

Suppose
B
contained
k
equal rows, indexed by
j_{1},\dots,j_{k}
. This means that
B_{j_{s}i}=B_{j_{t}i}
for all
i\in[n]
and
s,t\in[k]
. The rank-
k
projector

P=\sum_{s\in[k]}{|{j_{s}}\rangle}\!\bra{j_{s}}

then satisfies

PD_{i}P=\sum_{s,t\in[k]}{|{j_{s}}\rangle}\braket{j_{s}|D_{i}|j_{t}}\bra{j_{t}}=\sum_{s\in[k]}B_{j_{s}i}{|{j_{s}}\rangle}\!\bra{j_{s}}=\beta_{i}P

as desired.
∎

We hence get the following corollary regarding the independence number of
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
.

Corollary 4.31
.

We have
\alpha(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B})\geq\operatorname{EqRows}(B)
.

We can also lower bound
\alpha(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B})
in terms of
\rk B
. The proof is a nice application of
Tverberg’s theorem

[
41
]
, which states that any set of at least
1+(k-1)(r+1)
vectors in
\mathbb{R}^{r}
can be partitioned into
k
groups whose convex hulls share a common point. For what follows, it will be convenient to rephrase
Equation

18
in terms of isometries instead of projectors. Concretely,
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
has a
k
-independent set if and only if there exists an isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
such that

V^{\dagger}D_{i}V=\beta_{i}I_{k}

(19)

Equation

18
follows from
Equation

19
by multiplying both sides from the left with
V
and from the right with
V^{\dagger}
. Conversely, any isometry
V
with
\img V=\img P
satisfies
P=VV^{\dagger}
, so multiplying
Equation

18
from the left with
V^{\dagger}
and from the right with
V
recovers
Equation

19
.

Proposition 4.32
.

It holds that

\alpha(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B})\geq 1+\left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{\rk B+1}\right\rfloor.

Proof.

First, note that since we assume
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
to be undirected, it holds by
Proposition

3.10
that
\overline{B}=B
. Let
r\coloneqq\rk B
and let
k
be the right hand side of the ineqality in the statement. Our goal is to construct an isometry
V:\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
such that

V^{\dagger}\diag(B_{*i})V=\beta_{i}I_{k}\qquad\forall i\in[r],

(20)

for some
\beta_{i}\in\mathbb{R}
; actually we are going to construct below a
real
isometry
V
. The condition above implies, for all
s\in[k]
,

\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ji}\lvert V_{js}\rvert^{2}=\beta_{i}\qquad\forall i\in[r].

Since for a fixed
s
, the vector
(|V_{js}|^{2})_{j\in[n]}
is a probability vector, we can interpret the equation above as
\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{r}
lying in the convex hull of the vectors
B_{j*}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}
for
j\in[n]
.

To construct the (real) orthonormal vectors
v_{s}
and the vector
\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{r}
, we are going to apply Tverberg’s theorem. From the assumption in the statement we have
n\geq 1+(k-1)(r+1)
, hence we can partition the set
[n]
into
k
parts

[n]=J_{1}\sqcup J_{2}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup J_{k}

such that

\bigcap_{s=1}^{k}\operatorname{conv}\{B_{j*}\mid j\in J_{s}\}\neq\emptyset.

Let
\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{r}
be an arbitrary element of the intersection above. For all
s\in[k]
, we can write

\beta_{i}=\sum_{j\in J_{s}}p_{j}^{(s)}B_{ji}\qquad\forall i\in[r]

for some probability vector
p^{(s)}
. Now we define the isometry
V
as follows: for all
s\in[k]
and
j\in[n]
,

V_{js}\coloneqq\begin{cases}\sqrt{p^{(s)}_{j}}&\qquad\text{ if }j\in J_{s}\\
0&\qquad\text{ if }j\notin J_{s}.\end{cases}

First, note that the
k
column vectors
V_{*s}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
have unit norm by construction. Moreover, for
s\neq t
, it holds that
V_{*s}\perp V_{*t}
because they have disjoint supports. For any
s\in[k]
we have

[V^{\dagger}\diag(B_{*i})V]_{ss}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ji}|V_{js}|^{2}=\sum_{j\in J_{s}}B_{ji}p^{(s)}_{j}=\beta_{i}\qquad\forall i\in[r].

Using one more time the disjoint support property, we have for
s\neq t\in[k]
:

[V^{\dagger}\diag(B_{*i})V]_{st}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ji}V_{js}V_{jt}=0.

We have constructed thus an isometry as in (
20
), finishing the proof.
∎

We remark that the proof is conceptually very similar to that of Lemma 2.9 in
[
46
]
. In fact, we could have applied their result directly to obtain the bound: As required by their lemma, the operator systems corresponding to quantum graphs of the form
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
consist only of diagonal matrices. The only difference is that we need to account for the fact that our graphs do not have loops, which results in the
+1
in the denominator. We now proceed to prove a simple upper bound for the independence number that also depends on the rank of the matrix
B
.

Proposition 4.33
.

It holds that
\alpha(X_{\cdot,B})\leq n-\rk B
.

Proof.

Let
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
be an isometry witnessing the independence number of the quantum graph
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
with
k=\alpha(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B})
. Let
b_{1},\ldots,b_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
be vectors that span the image of the projection
B
. The isometry
V
satisfies

\forall i\in[r]\ \exists\beta_{i}\in\mathbb{R}\qquad V^{*}\diag(b_{i})V=\beta_{i}I_{k}.

(21)

Writing
c_{i}:=b_{i}-\beta_{i}\mathbf{1}
, the relation above can be re-written as
V^{*}\diag(c_{i})V=0
for
i\in[r]
. Setting
\mathcal{V}:=\img V
, we can rephrase the condition as

\diag(c_{i})\mathcal{V}\subseteq\mathcal{V}^{\perp}.

Pick a vector
v\in\mathcal{V}
having non-zero coordinates; if such a vector
v
does not exist, then
V
is effectively an isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{m}
with
m<n
and the bound in the statement can be improved to
\alpha(X_{\cdot,B})\leq m-r
. We have

d_{i}:=\diag(c_{i})v=\diag(v)c_{i}.

Since
\mathbf{1}\notin\img B
, the vectors
c_{1},\ldots c_{r}
are linearly independent, hence so are the vectors
d_{1},\ldots,d_{r}\in\mathcal{C}^{\perp}
, proving that
r\leq n-k
.
∎

Note that this upper bound nicely complements the lower bound in
Corollary

4.31
: A natural inequality is that
\rk B\leq n-\operatorname{EqRows}(B)+1
. For loopless
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
, we have
\mathbf{1}\in\ker B
, which implies that the column-sums of
B
must be
0
. The inequality thus becomes
\rk B\leq n-\operatorname{EqRows}(B)
, or equivalently
\operatorname{EqRows}(B)\leq n-\rk B
. Crucially, there exist projectors
B
that saturate this inequality. Take, for instance, the rank-
1
projection onto a vector
v
with
v_{1}=\dots=v_{n-1}=c
and
v_{n}=-(n-1)c
. It follows that there exist quantum graphs
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
for which our upper and lower bounds coincide.

Finally, note that a naive dimension count for the existence of a complex isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
witnessing the independence number of
X_{\cdot,B}
indicates that the real dimension of the complex Stiefel manifold of isometries
\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
needs to be larger than the total number of constraints in
Equation

21
:

2nk-k^{2}\geq r(k^{2}-1)\Longrightarrow k\leq\frac{n}{r+1}+\sqrt{\frac{n^{2}+r^{2}+r}{(r+1)^{2}}}.

We plot below the difference between the lower bound in
Proposition

4.32
and, respectively, the upper bound in
Proposition

4.33
(left panel) and the parameter cound in the equation above (right panel).

4.3.3
The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Cases

Given our knowledge of
\alpha(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C})
and
\alpha(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B})
, the treatment of the Symmetric and Antisymmetric quantum graphs is straightforward. The independence number of
G^{\mathrm{sym}}
can be determined using
Proposition

4.27
and the splitting principle, but it also follows from the more elemental proof below.

Proposition 4.34
.

It holds that
\alpha(G^{\mathrm{sym}})=1
.

Proof.

Every non-empty quantum graph has an independent set of size
1
, so it suffices to show that there exists no independent set of size
\geq 2
. Suppose that
P
is a projector witnessing an independent set. Then
P\neq 0
, so there exists an
i\in[n]
such that
P{|{i}\rangle}\neq 0
. Now the operator space corresponding to
G^{\mathrm{sym}}
plus
\mathbb{C}I
is spanned by
\{{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}+{|{j}\rangle}\!\bra{i}\mid i,j\in[n]\}
, so
P
in particular satisfies

P{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{i}P=c_{i}P.

Since
P{|{i}\rangle}\neq 0
, the left-hand side has rank
1
, which implies that
c_{i}\neq 0
and
\rk P=1
.
∎

The case for the Antisymmetric quantum graph is again an immediate corollary of
Proposition

4.27
.

Proposition 4.35
.

It holds that
\alpha(G^{\mathrm{asym}})=1
.

Proof.

G^{\mathrm{asym}}
is of the form
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}
so
Proposition

4.27
applies. By
Proposition

3.18
the strange graph corresponding to
G^{\mathrm{asym}}
is a complete graph, which has independence number
1
.
∎

4.3.4
The Complete and Empty Graphs

We conclude with the independence numbers of the complete and the empty quantum graphs.

Proposition 4.36
.

We have
\alpha(K_{n}^{c})=n
and
\alpha(K_{n})=1
.

Proof.

The operator space corresponding to
K_{n}^{c}
is the trivial space, so any projector
P
satisfies
PSP\subseteq P
, in particular this holds for
P=I
. The complete graph satisfies
K_{n}=X_{\tfrac{nJ-I}{n},\tfrac{nI-J}{n}}
, so its corresponding strange graph is the complete graph with only classical edges.
Proposition

4.26
thus implies that
\alpha(K_{n})\leq 1
. The trivial lower bound
\alpha(K_{n})\geq 1
then establishes the equality.
∎

4.4
Cliques

Finally, we want to turn our attention to cliques. We will find it more convenient to phrase the definition of cliques in terms of isometries instead of projectors. As such, a
k
-clique of a loopless quantum graph with operator space
S
is given by an isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
such that
V^{\dagger}(S\oplus\mathbb{C}I)V=M_{k}
. This rephrasing suggests the following strategy to prove the (non-)existence of
k
-cliques. Let
P_{S}\colon M_{n}\to M_{n}
be the projector onto
S
. Then an isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
gives a
k
-clique if and only if the map

L_{V}\colon M_{n}\oplus\mathbb{C}\to M_{k},(x,\alpha)\mapsto V^{\dagger}(P_{S}(x)+\alpha I)V

has full image. Since
(\img L_{V})^{\bot}=\ker L_{V}^{\dagger}
, this is happens if and only if
L_{V}^{\dagger}
has trivial kernel. Now we have

\langle(x,\alpha),L_{V}^{\dagger}(y)\rangle=\langle L_{V}(x,\alpha),y\rangle=\langle V^{\dagger}P_{S}(x)V,y\rangle+\overline{\alpha}\langle I,y\rangle=\langle x,P_{S}(VyV^{\dagger})\rangle+\overline{\alpha}\Tr y

for all
x\in M_{n}
,
\alpha\in\mathbb{C}
. This implies that an arbitrary
y\in M_{k}
is in the kernel of
L_{V}^{\dagger}
if and only if
P_{S}(VyV^{\dagger})=0
and
\Tr y=0
. To find a
k
-clique it is thus necessary and sufficient to find an isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
such that there are no traceless
y\in M_{k}
in the kernel of
x\mapsto P_{S}(VxV^{\dagger})
.

Proposition 4.37
.

Given a quantum graph with operator space
S
, the clique number
\omega
is given by

\omega=\max\{k\mid\exists V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}\text{ isometry such that }\big[\Tr y=0\text{ and }P_{S}(VyV^{\dagger})=0\big]\Rightarrow y=0\}.

4.4.1
ABC Graphs

We will not be able to prove bounds for
X_{A,B,C}
in terms of
A,B,C
, but we are able to extend the splitting principle proved in the case of independent sets (see
Proposition

4.26
) to cliques.

Proposition 4.38
.

Let
X_{A,B,C}
be a quantum graph. Then we have
\omega(X_{A,B,C})\geq\max\{\omega(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}),\omega(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B})\}
.

Proof.

Denote the operator spaces of
X_{A,B,C}
,
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}
, and
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
by
S_{ABC}
,
S_{AC}
, and
S_{B}
respectively. Recall from the proof of
Proposition

3.10
that the projector onto
S_{ABC}
decomposes as

(X_{A,B,C})^{R}=X_{B,A,C}=B\oplus\bigoplus_{i<j}\begin{pmatrix}A_{ij}&C_{ij}\\
C_{ji}&A_{ji}\end{pmatrix}.

The
B
-summand is the projector onto
S_{B}
, while the remaining summands form the projector onto
S_{AC}
. Since the image of a direct sum is the direct sum of the images, we have
S_{ABC}=S_{AC}\oplus S_{B}
, and in particular
S_{ABC}\supseteq S_{AC}
and
S_{ABC}\supseteq S_{B}
. Now suppose
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
witnesses a
k
-clique of
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}
, i.e.
V^{\dagger}(S_{AC}\oplus\mathbb{C}I)V=M_{k}
. Since
S_{ABC}\supseteq S_{AC}
, we have

M_{k}=V^{\dagger}(S_{AC}\oplus\mathbb{C}I)V\subseteq V^{\dagger}(S_{ABC}\oplus\mathbb{C}I)V\subseteq M_{k},

so
V
also witnesses a
k
-clique of
X_{A,B,C}
. The same argument with
S_{B}
in place of
S_{AC}
yields the result. ∎

4.4.2
AB Graphs

Moving on to AB graphs, we start with the case of
X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B}
. It turns out that we can upper bound
\omega(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B})
in terms of
\rk B
.

.

It holds that
\omega(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B})\leq\sqrt{\rk B+1}

where
d_{y}\coloneqq\diag VyV^{\dagger}
. Let
T\coloneqq\{\diag VyV^{\dagger}\mid y\in M_{k},\Tr y=0\}
. The question then becomes under which conditions we can find an isometry
V
such that
(i)
\diag VyV^{\dagger}\neq 0

for all non-zero traceless
y\in M_{k}
and (ii)
T\cap\ker B=\{0\}
.

Note that condition (ii) is satisfied if and only if for every basis
t_{1},\dots,t_{\ell}
of
T
and
b_{1},\dots,b_{\ell^{\prime}}
of
\ker B
the set
\{t_{1},\dots,t_{\ell},b_{1},\dots,b_{\ell^{\prime}}\}
is linearly independent. It is thus necessary that
\dim T\leq n-\dim\ker B=\rk B
. Condition (i) on the other hand is equivalent to the map
\Phi_{V}\colon\mathfrak{sl}_{k}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathbb{C}^{n},x\mapsto\diag VxV^{\dagger}
being injective. It follows that
\dim T=\rk\Phi_{V}=\dim\mathfrak{sl}_{k}(\mathbb{C})=k^{2}-1
, and thus
k\leq\sqrt{\rk B+1}
.
∎

It turns out that this upper bound can generally be achieved, and this question is closely related to the existence of specific
informationally complete POVMs
(IC-POVMs, see e.g.
[
24
, Section 3.3]
). The easiest case is
B=I-J/n
.

Proposition 4.40
.

Let
B=I-J/n
. Then
\omega(X_{\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},B})=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor
.

Proof.

We have
\ker B=\lspan\{\mathbf{1}\}
, where
\mathbf{1}=(1,\dots,1)^{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}
. The upper bound on the clique number follows from
Proposition

4.39
. For the lower bound, we shall use the same proof strategy as in
Proposition

4.39
: It suffices to show that for
k=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor
there exists an isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
satisfying the following conditions:

(i)

\diag VyV^{\dagger}\neq 0
for all non-zero traceless
y\in M_{k}

(ii)

\{\diag VyV^{\dagger}\mid y\in M_{k},\Tr y=0\}\cap\ker B=\{0\}
.

We first observe that condition (ii) is automatically satisfied whenever condition (i) holds. Indeed, let
y\in M_{k}
be traceless and let
v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{C}^{k}
denote the rows of
V
, so that
(\diag VyV^{\dagger})_{i}=v_{i}^{\dagger}yv_{i}
. Then

\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\diag VyV^{\dagger})_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}^{\dagger}yv_{i}=\Tr\left(y\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}v_{i}^{\dagger}\right)=\Tr(y)=0,

where we used that
\sum_{i}v_{i}v_{i}^{\dagger}=I_{k}
since
V
is an isometry. In other words, the image of
\Phi_{V}
on traceless matrices is contained in the hyperplane
\mathbf{1}^{\bot}=(\ker B)^{\bot}
. Thus for any non-zero traceless
y
satisfying
\diag VyV^{\dagger}\neq 0
, the vector
\diag VyV^{\dagger}
cannot lie in
\ker B=\lspan\{\mathbf{1}\}
, and condition (ii) is automatic.
The problem therefore reduces to finding the largest
k
for which condition (i) can be satisfied: The map
\Phi_{V}\colon\mathfrak{sl}_{k}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
,
x\mapsto\diag VxV^{\dagger}
, must be injective.

It remains to show that for
k=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor
, an isometry satisfying condition (i) exists. Set
m=k^{2}\leq n
. We will construct
n
vectors
v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{C}^{k}
with
\sum_{i}v_{i}v_{i}^{\dagger}=I_{k}
whose rank-one operators
v_{i}v_{i}^{\dagger}
span
M_{k}
. Note that this is the defining property of an IC-POVM. Consider the standard basis
{|{1}\rangle},\dots,{|{k}\rangle}
of
\mathbb{C}^{k}
, and define the following
m=k^{2}
vectors:

1.

The
k
basis vectors
{|{1}\rangle},\dots,{|{k}\rangle}
.

2.

For each pair
1\leq s<t\leq k
, the vector
({|{s}\rangle}+{|{t}\rangle})/\sqrt{2}
.

3.

For each pair
1\leq s<t\leq k
, the vector
({|{s}\rangle}+i{|{t}\rangle})/\sqrt{2}
.

This gives
k+2\binom{k}{2}=k^{2}
vectors. Their rank-one outer products span
M_{k}
: The vectors in (a) yield the diagonal matrix units
{|{s}\rangle}\!\bra{s}
; the vectors in (b) yield operators whose off-diagonal part is proportional to
{|{s}\rangle}\!\bra{t}+{|{t}\rangle}\!\bra{s}
(recovering the real parts of off-diagonal matrix units); and the vectors in (c) yield operators whose off-diagonal part is proportional to
i({|{s}\rangle}\!\bra{t}-{|{t}\rangle}\!\bra{s})
(recovering the imaginary parts). Together these span all of
M_{k}
.
Denote these
m
vectors by
w_{1},\dots,w_{m}
and let

F\coloneqq\sum_{l=1}^{m}w_{l}w_{l}^{\dagger}.

Since the operators
w_{l}w_{l}^{\dagger}
span
M_{k}
, the matrix
F
is positive definite. Set
u_{l}\coloneqq F^{-1/2}w_{l}
for each
l
. Then

\sum_{l=1}^{m}u_{l}u_{l}^{\dagger}=F^{-1/2}\left(\sum_{l}w_{l}w_{l}^{\dagger}\right)F^{-1/2}=I_{k}.

Moreover, the operators
u_{l}u_{l}^{\dagger}=F^{-1/2}w_{l}w_{l}^{\dagger}F^{-1/2}
still span
M_{k}
, since conjugation by the invertible matrix
F^{-1/2}
preserves linear independence.

If
m=n
, we set
v_{l}=u_{l}
and are done. If
m<n
, we extend the collection to
n
vectors as follows. Choose any
u_{1}\neq 0
and split it into
n-m+1
copies: Set
v_{l}=u_{1}/\sqrt{n-m+1}
for
l=1,\dots,n-m+1
, and
v_{l}=u_{l-n+m}
for
l=n-m+2,\dots,n
. These
n
vectors still satisfy
\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}v_{i}^{\dagger}=I_{k}
, and the set
\{v_{i}v_{i}^{\dagger}\}
still spans
M_{k}
since it contains all the original
u_{l}u_{l}^{\dagger}
(up to rescaling
u_{1}u_{1}^{\dagger}
, which remains non-zero).
We thus obtain an isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
with having the vectors
v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{C}^{k}
as rows:

V=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{v_{i}}.

For any traceless
y\in M_{k}
,

\Phi_{V}(y)_{i}=v_{i}^{\dagger}yv_{i}=\Tr(v_{i}v_{i}^{\dagger}\cdot y)=\Tr\left((v_{i}v_{i}^{\dagger}-\frac{\|v_{i}\|^{2}}{k}I_{k})\cdot y\right),

where the last equality uses
\Tr(y)=0
. The centred operators
v_{i}v_{i}^{\dagger}-\|v_{i}\|^{2}I_{k}/k
are traceless, and they span all of
\mathfrak{sl}_{k}(\mathbb{C})
since the
v_{i}v_{i}^{\dagger}
span
M_{k}
. If
\Phi_{V}(y)=0
, then
y
is orthogonal (in the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product) to every
v_{i}v_{i}^{\dagger}-\|v_{i}\|^{2}I_{k}/k
, hence to all of
\mathfrak{sl}_{k}(\mathbb{C})
. Since
y
is itself traceless, this forces
y=0
. Thus
\Phi_{V}
is injective, establishing condition (i).
∎

The case for
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
is curious. Given our previous results, we would expect that
\omega(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})=\omega(A)
. However, this is not the case. Weaver had already noticed this discrepancy in
[
45
]
: Recall that he works with operator spaces that correspond to quantum graphs with loops at every vertex. One such operator space is
D_{n}
, the space of all diagonal matrices. He proves the following.

Proposition 4.41

(Proposition 2.2 in
[
45
]
)
.

If
n\geq k^{2}+k-1
then
D_{n}
has a
k
-clique.

Consider the empty graph with loops at every vertex. Just as for loopless graphs, we can consider the quantum graph
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
, which in this case is equal to
X_{A,I}
(note that this quantum graph has loops since
\mathbf{1}\not\in\ker B
). The corresponding operator space is given precisely by
\img X^{R}_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}=D_{n}
. Weaver’s result can thus be interpreted as the empty graph on
n
vertices having a
k
-clique if
n
is large enough. The problem persists when restricting to loopless quantum graphs.

Proposition 4.42
.

Let
A
be the adjacency matrix of the complete classical graph. Then
\omega(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})<\omega(A)
.

Proof.

The projector onto the operator space corresponding to
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
is given by

-

The operator space is thus given by

S=\lspan\{{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}\mid i\neq j\in[n]\},

the space of all matrices with zero diagonal. We have
\omega(A)=n
. If there were an
n
-clique, there would be an isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
such that
V(S\oplus\mathbb{C}I)V^{\dagger}=M_{n}
. This is impossible, since
\dim M_{n}=n^{2}>n^{2}-n+1=\dim S\oplus\mathbb{C}I
.
∎

There are also loopless graphs for which
\omega(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})>\omega(A)
. In fact, the former can be arbitrarily larger.

Proposition 4.43
.

Let
A
be the adjacency matrix of the classical complete bipartite graph. Then
\omega(A)=2
and
\omega(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})\geq n/2
.

Proof.

It is straightforward to see that the complete bipartite graph has clique number
2
, since any larger clique must contain an odd cycle. The operator space
S
corresponding to
\omega(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})
is spanned by the non-zero coordinates of the matrix

A=\begin{pmatrix}0&J\\
J&0\end{pmatrix}.

Choosing the isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{n/2}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
as

V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}I\\
I\end{pmatrix},

we get
V^{\dagger}SV=M_{k}
and thus in particular
V^{\dagger}(S\oplus\mathbb{C}I)V=M_{k}
.
∎

In general, we can slightly lower the trivial upper bound on
\omega(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})
from
n
to
n-1
, but not any further.

Proposition 4.44
.

For all
A
, we have
\omega(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})\leq n-1
. If
A
is the adjacency matrix of the complete classical graph, then
\omega(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})=n-1
.

Proof.

Since the operator space
S
associated to
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
is a coordinate subspace of
M_{n}
, and
A
has zero diagonal, we have
\dim(S\oplus\mathbb{C}I)\leq n^{2}-n+1
. It follows that for any isometry
V
,
\dim V^{\dagger}(S\oplus\mathbb{C}I)V\leq n^{2}-n+1<n^{2}
, so
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
cannot have an
n
-clique.

We now claim that if
S
is maximal subject to these constraints, that is

S=\lspan\{{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}\mid i,j\in[n],i\neq j\},

then there exists an isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{n-1}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
such that for all
y\in M_{n-1}
with
\Tr y=0
we have

P_{S}(VyV^{\dagger})=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=0.

(22)

Proposition

4.37
then implies that if
A
is the complete classical graph then
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
has a clique of size
n-1
.

Let
y\in M_{n-1}
be arbitrary and let
Q\coloneq VyV^{\dagger}
. Then
y=V^{\dagger}QV
and thus
Q=VV^{\dagger}QVV^{\dagger}=RQR
, where
R
is the projector onto
\img V
. Now
R
has rank
n-1
, so it is of the form

R=I-uu^{\dagger}

for some unit-norm
u\in\mathbb{C}^{n}
. Choose
u=1/\sqrt{n}\mathbf{1}
. Suppose then that
P_{S}(VyV^{\dagger})=P_{S}(Q)=0
. Then
Q\in S^{\bot}=D_{n}
. Then
\diag Q=Q\mathbf{1}=RQR\mathbf{1}=0
. Since
Q
is diagonal, this implies that
Q=0
and thus
y=V^{\dagger}QV=0
as required.
∎

Despite
Proposition

4.42
, there is some hope for lower bounds on
\omega(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})
in terms of
\omega(A)
. It turns out that the lower bound just barely fails. Concretely, we can prove the following.

Proposition 4.45
.

It holds that
\omega(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})\geq\omega(A)-1
.

Proof.

Let
k=\omega(A)
. Then the classical graph
A
has a clique of size
k
. Concretely, there exists a set
C\subseteq[n]
, such that
A_{ij}=1
for all
i\neq j\in C
. For the operator space
S
of
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
, this implies that

\lspan\{{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}\mid i,j\in C,i\neq j\}\subseteq\lspan S.

Enumerate the elements of
C
as
c_{1},\dots,c_{k}
, and define an isometry
W
by

W=\sum_{i=1}^{k}{|{c_{i}}\rangle}\!\bra{i}.

Then
W^{\dagger}SW=\lspan\{{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}\mid i\neq j\in[k]\}\subseteq M_{k}
. But this is the operator space of
X_{K_{k},\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
! By
Proposition

4.44
, we know that there exists an isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k-1}\to\mathbb{C}^{k}
such that
V^{\dagger}(W^{\dagger}SW\oplus\mathbb{C}I_{k})V=M_{k-1}
. We also have
W^{\dagger}I_{n}W=I_{k}
, so

W^{\dagger}(S\oplus\mathbb{C}I_{n})W=W^{\dagger}SW\oplus\mathbb{C}I_{k}.

It follows that

V^{\dagger}W^{\dagger}(S\oplus\mathbb{C}I_{n})WV=V^{\dagger}(W^{\dagger}SW\oplus\mathbb{C}I_{k})V=M_{k-1},

so
WV\colon\mathbb{C}^{k-1}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
witnesses a clique of size
k-1
.
∎

One may wonder why
\omega(A)
fails to be a lower bound by such a close margin. We can shed some light on this by considering the role of loops, and the different operator spaces that may be associated to a classical graph. Recall that Weaver’s original definition of a
k
-clique requires the existence of a rank-
k
projector such that
PSP=PM_{n}P
, where
S
is the operator space associated to the quantum graph. As Weaver mentions in
[
47
]
, the operator space
S
should be seen as the edge relation of the quantum graph (in analogy to the edge relation
E(G)\subseteq V(G)\times V(G)
of a classical graph
G
), while the “sandwiching” operation
PSP
should be seen as a restriction of a relation to some subset of the underlying set. In terms of classical graphs, the condition
PSP=PM_{n}P
may thus be interpreted as the existence of an induced subgraph that is isomorphic to an induced subgraph of the complete graph with loops at all vertices (the largest possible relation).

This seems to suggest that intuitively, we need our quantum graph to have loops in order to find cliques.
4
4

4

This is not actually true, as the proof of
Proposition

4.43
shows. This is because the mental model of viewing
PSP
as the restriction of a relation to some set is already not rigorous. Nevertheless, it will suffice for the point we are making.
However, the quantum graphs that we are considering do not have loops.
To address this issue, we have modified the definition of cliques to require the existence of a projection
P
with
P(S\oplus\mathbb{C}I)P=PM_{n}P
. Adding the identity to the operator space of a loopless quantum graph yields a quantum graph with loops at every vertex, which then allows us to use Weaver’s definition. This way of adding loops is very natural, because the resulting operator space is the smallest superspace of
S
that has loops at every vertex.

The problem arises when considering quantum graphs of the form
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
. We have seen in
Corollary

3.12
that
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
is loopless if and only if
A
is loopless, and adding the identity to the corresponding operator space turns it into a quantum graph with loops at every vertex as desired. However, there is a second natural way to add these loops. Namely, we can add the loops to the classical graph
A
, letting
A^{\circ}=A+I
, and then consider
X_{A^{\circ},\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}}
. This does not result in the same operator space. The former approach yields

S^{\prime}=S\oplus\mathbb{C}I=\lspan(\{{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}\mid A_{ij}\neq 0\}\cup\{I\})

while the latter approach yields

S^{\circ}=\lspan\{{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}\mid A_{ij}\neq 0\text{ or }i=j\}.

Concretely,
S^{\circ}
contains the diagonal elements
{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{i}
for
i\in[n]
, while
S^{\prime}
does not. Otherwise
S^{\prime}
and
S^{\circ}
are the same. We thus expect
S^{\circ}
to have larger cliques. This suggests that
S^{\circ}
instead of
S^{\prime}
might be the more natural choice to upper bound
\omega(A)
.

Conveniently, our framework allows us to recover
S^{\circ}
exactly. Let us consider some arbitrary loopless classical graph
A
and consider
X_{A+\diag(1-1/n),B}
for
B=I-J/n
.
5
5

5

This choice of
B
has non-zero diagonal, so we need to add the diagonal to
A
as well. This is merely a notational quirk, since the diagonal is removed again in the resulting linear map.
Then the projector
X^{R}_{A+\diag(1-1/n),B}
onto the operator space is given by

It is not hard to see that this projector precisely has image
S^{\circ}
: The first term provides
S
, while the second term provides the diagonal elements. And indeed, we find that its clique number is lower bounded by
\omega(A)
.

Proposition 4.46
.

If
A
is the adjacency matrix of a graph
G
, then
\omega(X_{A+\mathrm{diag}(1-1/n),I-J/n})\geq\omega(G)
.

Proof.

Let
k=\omega(G)
and let
C=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{k}\}\subseteq[n]
be a
k
-clique of
G
, so that
A_{c_{s}c_{t}}=1
for all
s\neq t
. Define the isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
by
V{|{s}\rangle}={|{c_{s}}\rangle}
. Recall from the discussion above that
S\oplus\mathbb{C}I=S^{\circ}=\lspan\{{|{i}\rangle}\!\bra{j}\mid A_{ij}\neq 0\text{ or }i=j\}
. For all
s,t\in[k]
, the matrix unit
{|{c_{s}}\rangle}\!\bra{c_{t}}
lies in
S^{\circ}
: If
s\neq t
, this follows from
A_{c_{s}c_{t}}=1
, and if
s=t
from the diagonal condition. Since
V^{\dagger}{|{c_{s}}\rangle}\!\bra{c_{t}}V={|{s}\rangle}\!\bra{t}
, it follows that
V^{\dagger}S^{\circ}V=M_{k}
, so
V
witnesses a
k
-clique of
X_{A+\mathrm{diag}(1-1/n),I-J/n}
. ∎

4.4.3
The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Cases

For the symmetric and antisymmetric quantum graphs, we can determine
\omega
exactly.

Proposition 4.47
.

The clique number of the Symmetric and the Antisymmetric quantum graphs on
n
vertices is

\omega(G^{\mathrm{sym}})=\omega(G^{\mathrm{asym}})=\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil.

Proof.

Let
P_{S}^{a}
and
P_{S}^{s}
be the projection onto the operator spaces of
G^{\mathrm{asym}}
and
G^{\mathrm{sym}}
respectively. By
Proposition

4.37
, we want to determine the maximum
k
such that there exists an isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
with
P_{S}^{a}(VyV^{\dagger})\neq 0
respectively
P_{S}^{s}(VyV^{\dagger})\neq 0
for all traceless non-zero matrices
y\in M_{k}
. Concretely, the conditions become

P_{S}^{a}(VyV^{\dagger})
=
V
\overline{V}
y
V
\overline{V}
y
-
\neq
0

and

P_{S}^{s}(VyV^{\dagger})
=
V
\overline{V}
y
V
\overline{V}
y
+
\neq
0.
-
\frac{2}{n}
y
V
\overline{V}
y
V
\overline{V}
y
+
=

We thus want to understand under which conditions the map

P_{X}
\overline{V}
V
L_{V}
=

has traceless matrices in its kernel, where
X\in\{\operatorname{Sym},\operatorname{Asym}\}
. First note that
V\otimes\overline{V}
maps
y\mapsto VyV^{\dagger}
and thus preserves the trace. We need to find a traceless
x\in\img(V\otimes\overline{V})\cap X^{\bot}
.

First consider
X=\operatorname{Sym}
. We have
x\in\img(V\otimes\overline{V})
if and only if
x=Vy\overline{V}^{\mathsf{T}}
.
This in turn is equivalent to
\img x\subseteq\img V
and
\img x^{\mathsf{T}}\subseteq\img\overline{V}
. Now if
x
is required to be antisymmetric then
\img x^{\mathsf{T}}=-\img x=\img x
.
We thus need to determine when there exists an antisymmetric
x\in M_{n}
with
\img x\subseteq\img V\cap\img\overline{V}
. Let
S_{V}\coloneqq\img V\cap\img\overline{V}
. If
\dim S_{V}\geq 2
, such an
x
exists. Indeed, choose orthogonal
\psi_{1},\psi_{2}\in S_{V}
and let

x=\psi_{1}\psi_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}-\psi_{2}\psi_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}.

Then
x
is antisymmetric (and thus automatically traceless) and
\img x\subseteq\img S_{V}
as desired. On the other hand, if
\dim S_{V}<2
then no such non-zero map exists because there are no rank
1
asymmetric matrices.

The story is analogous for
X=\operatorname{Asym}
. We are looking for a traceless symmetric
x\in\img(V\otimes\overline{V})
. Since
\img x^{\mathsf{T}}=\img x
, we again require
\img x\subseteq\img V\cap\img\overline{V}=S_{V}
. For
\dim S_{V}\geq 2
, we may choose

x=\psi_{1}\psi_{2}^{\dagger}+\overline{\psi_{2}}\psi_{1}^{\mathsf{T}},

which is symmetric and satisfies the image condition since
S_{V}
is closed under conjugation. Moreover,
x
is traceless: We have

\displaystyle\Tr\psi_{1}\psi_{2}^{\dagger}+\overline{\psi_{2}}\psi_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}

\displaystyle=\Tr\psi_{1}\psi_{2}^{\dagger}+\Tr\overline{\psi_{2}}\psi_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}

\displaystyle=\langle\psi_{2},\psi_{1}\rangle+\langle\overline{\psi_{1}},\overline{\psi_{2}}\rangle

\displaystyle=2\langle\psi_{2},\psi_{1}\rangle=0.

Conversely, if
\dim S_{V}<2
no such non-zero
x
exists. If
S_{V}=\mathbb{C}\psi
, the only choice is

x=\psi\psi^{\mathsf{T}}

which has trace
\langle\overline{\psi},\psi\rangle\neq 0
.

We have shown that
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
witnesses a
k
-clique if and only if
\dim S_{V}<2
. We first show that this is unsatisfiable for
k>\lceil n/2\rceil
. It holds that

\dim S_{V}=\dim(\img V\cap\img\overline{V})=\dim\img V+\dim\img\overline{V}-\dim(\img V+\img\overline{V}).

Since
V
is an isometry, we have
\rk V=\rk\overline{V}=k
. We thus have
\dim S_{V}<2
if and only if
2k-\dim(\img V\oplus\img\overline{V})<2
, or equivalently

2k-2<\dim(\img V\oplus\img\overline{V})\leq n.

(23)

This is only satisfiable if

k\leq\frac{n+1}{2}.

For
n
odd, we have

\frac{n+1}{2}=\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil

while for
n
even and
k\in\mathbb{N}
we have

k\leq\frac{n+1}{2}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad k\leq\frac{n}{2}=\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil,

which yields the desired bound. Conversely, let
k=\lceil n/2\rceil
and choose a random isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
. Then
\dim(\img V+\img\overline{V})=n-\dim(\img V\cap\img\overline{V})=n
by the lemma below. This completes the proof.
∎

Lemma 4.48
.

Let
1\leq k\leq n/2
. If
E
is a Haar-distributed random
k
-dimensional complex subspace of
\mathbb{C}^{n}
, then

E\cap\overline{E}=\{0\}

almost surely.

Proof.

We generate a random
k
-dimensional subspace
E\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{n}
as the range of a complex Ginibre matrix. Let
A\in M_{n\times k}(\mathbb{C})
be a matrix whose entries are independent complex Gaussian random variables. With probability one,
A
has rank
k
, and its column space
E=\operatorname{im}(A)
is a random element of the complex Grassmannian with the unitarily invariant distribution.

Suppose that
E\cap\overline{E}\neq\{0\}
. Then there exists
v\neq 0
such that
v\in E\cap\overline{E}
and thus there exist vectors
x,y\in\mathbb{C}^{k}
, not both zero, such that
v=Ax=\overline{A}y
. Equivalently,
Ax-\overline{A}y=0
. Define the matrix

M(A)=\begin{bmatrix}A&-\overline{A}\end{bmatrix}\in M_{n\times 2k}(\mathbb{C}).

Then the above condition becomes

M(A)\begin{pmatrix}x\\
y\end{pmatrix}=0.

Thus
E\cap\overline{E}\neq\{0\}
if and only if
\ker M(A)\neq\{0\}
, or equivalently
\operatorname{rank}M(A)<2k
.
Since
k\leq n/2
, we have
2k\leq n
, so
M(A)
can have full column rank
2k
. The condition
\operatorname{rank}M(A)<2k
is equivalent to the vanishing of all
2k\times 2k
minors of
M(A)
, which are polynomial functions of the real and imaginary parts of the entries of
A
. Since the entries of
A
are independent continuous random variables, to show that the probability that these polynomial vanish is zero we need to prove that the polynomials are not identically zero.

To this end, we shall exhibit a matrix
A
with
\operatorname{rank}M(A)=2k
. Consider the deterministic matrix

A=\begin{bmatrix}I_{k}\\
iI_{k}\\
0\end{bmatrix}\in M_{n\times k}(\mathbb{C}),

where the last block has size
(n-2k)\times k
. Then

M(A)=\begin{bmatrix}I_{k}&-I_{k}\\
iI_{k}&iI_{k}\\
0&0\end{bmatrix}.

If

M(A)\begin{pmatrix}x\\
y\end{pmatrix}=0,

then
x-y=0
and
ix+iy=0
which gives
x=y=0
. Therefore
\ker M(A)=\{0\}
and
\operatorname{rank}M(A)=2k
for our choice of
A
, finishing the proof.
∎

4.4.4
The Complete and Empty Graphs

We conclude by considering the empty and the complete graph. We have seen that the operator space corresponding to the empty graph is
S_{K^{c}}=0
, while the operator space
S_{K}
corresponding to the complete graph is the set of all traceless matrices. In the former case, we have
S_{K^{c}}\oplus\mathbb{C}I=\mathbb{C}I
. It follows that any isometry
V\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
satisfies
V^{\dagger}(S_{K^{c}}\oplus\mathbb{C}I)V=M_{1}
and we cannot do any better by dimensionality. On the other hand, we have
S_{K}\oplus\mathbb{C}I=M_{n}
, so the identity is an isometry
\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}
witnessing a clique of size
n
. We can thus state the final result of our graph theoretic investigation.

Proposition 4.49
.

We have
\omega(K_{n})=n
and
\omega(K_{n}^{c})=1
.

Note that while we only list graph properties, we have in certain cases proved even stronger results, such as correspondences between the quantum graph structure and structure of matrices or classical graphs. We have also proved stronger bounds in certain special cases that we do not list for the sake of legibility.

5
Conclusion

In this work, we have introduced and systematically studied families of quantum graphs on
M_{n}
that are invariant under the action of classical matrix groups. By considering the chain of subgroups
U(n)\supseteq O(n)\supseteq\operatorname{Hyp}(n)\supseteq DO(n)\subseteq DU(n)
, we have shown that progressively smaller symmetry groups give rise to progressively richer classes of quantum graphs, mirroring the classical situation. Our main conceptual contribution is the parametrisation of
DU(n)
- and
DO(n)
-invariant quantum graphs by triples of matrices
(A,B,C)
, building on previous work in quantum information theory
[
39
,
32
]
.
This parametrisation reveals a clean separation of roles of the three matrices:
A
encodes a classical graph (
Corollary

3.12
),
C
introduces
strange edges
carrying a phase (
Proposition

3.18
), and
B
provides a purely quantum contribution with no classical analogue. We call the resulting classical model the strange graph
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
. Importantly, we prove a
splitting principle
that decomposes graph-theoretic conditions into independent conditions on the
(A,C)
and
B
parts.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that large, parametric families of non-trivial quantum graphs have been exhibited for which standard graph parameters such as the number of connected components, the independence number, the clique number, and the chromatic number, can all be computed or tightly bounded analytically. Our work provides a rich source of examples, counterexamples, and a guiding framework for future study of quantum graph theory.

Several questions remain open. The clique number of general ABC graphs
X_{A,B,C}
remains undetermined (see
Propositions

4.39
and
4.44
for the partial results obtained in this work), as do tight bounds on the chromatic number of
X_{A,B}
in terms of
A
and
B
. The difficulty of this problem lies in the very complex interaction between the strange graph parts described by the matrices
A
and
C
, and the purely quantum parts described by the projector
B
.

Another direction concerns the connectedness equivalence established in
Proposition

4.15
: while connectedness of
X_{A,B,C}
and of the strange graph
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
agree for
n\geq 3
, the correspondence breaks down at the level of connected components, as shown by
Proposition

4.13
. It would be interesting to determine the exact number of connected components of
X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}},C}
in terms of
\mathfrak{G}(A,C)
, and in particular to understand the role played by isolated strange edges with phase
\pi
. More broadly, the quantum clique number
\omega(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})
can differ from the classical clique number
\omega(A)
in both directions, and the precise relationship between these two quantities remains unclear beyond the bound
\omega(X_{A,\makebox[3.01389pt]{{$\cdot$}}})\geq\omega(A)-1
.

A natural next step is to consider
quantum
symmetries instead. It is known that the quantum symmetries of
M_{n}
are given by the projective free unitary quantum group
PU_{n}^{+}

[
2
, Corollary 4.1]
. It would thus be interesting to consider which classes of quantum graphs are acted on by quantum subgroups of
PU_{n}^{+}
, and whether they can also be described in discrete terms.
